These days I have been rewriting my Sunflower novella with remarkable success. I am handwriting it, with a pencil, and a margin. I open the notebook at any moment of the day and write each scene in about five minutes. This is very practical with work and children. Me and my partner have seasons of Anime binging in the evenings, which means I read much less than I otherwise would; but it is time with him, that matters. The little time I have between kids' bedtime and partner's time, I write on bed.  

I try to write eight A5 pages a day on working days; which equals 1,000 good words. I write when they watch their morning shows, as I arrive to work, on coffee breaks and lunch. I also try to write before I go home, since once I get home, I work much more than in my actual job — the chores of a Homemaker. items.title: Eight, or is it nine?
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Tuvalu is a micronation in the middle of the Pacific Ocean which was part of the British protectorate of Gilbert & Ellis Islands from 1892 to 1976. The rather enchanting memoir A Pattern of  Islands (1952) by Arthur Grimble, who administered there 1914 - 1933, is no longer read - there are only 2 copies available in Irish Public Libraries. I have, or used to have, a copy. Achieving independence aka being dumped from the British colonial portfolio was preceded by a certain amount of racial aggro between the Melanesian Gilbertese and the Polynesian Ellice Islanders. A plebiscite determined that each group formed separate nations Kiribati vs Tuvalu. Tuvalu is a parliamentary democracy in the UK tradition and King Charles Windsor is the Head of State. Having a seat at the UN is kinda nutso because the entire population (~10,660) of Tuvalu could fit in a modest provincial football stadium. Even Leitrim, Ireland's least populous county has 3x more people. fwiw Kiribati…

items.title: Hopi corn and chokecherry gravy: feeding students’ taste for native foods, culture
items.label: Hobbies and Creative
items.excerpt:
The tall, dense stalks of blue Hopi corn were a burst of green among the dry grassland of southeastern Wyoming. As the small patch of crops whipped in the wind, Lisa Ansell Frazier led the way into the rows and gently touched the leaves, tassels and budding silk. If you talk to the corn and say hi, she said, it will reach out and touch you.

“These are our babies,” she said. “This is the corn that is going to our schools.”

On a hot August afternoon, the corn still had weeks to mature alongside Huckleberry Gold potatoes and Jerusalem artichokes on the Mitákuye Ówahe Farm near Cheyenne. The produce would eventually travel more than 300 miles west to the Wind River Reservation, where it would be delivered to schools and pantries called food lodges.

The farm is just one facet of the Buffalo Youth Nation Project, a Wyoming nonprofit working to restore food sovereignty — which ensures Indigenous communities have the right to make decisions about what they grow, harvest and eat, according…

items.title: The Search Committee
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Two big, long-in-the-making additions to this site today. Whee!

The first is the addition of House committees and their transcripts. Committees can be really interesting. Even though this current Parliament certainly doesn't mark their heyday, they're still the most productive part of the House. There's way less theatre and name-calling than in debates—and, unlike in the House chamber, nobody's ever speaking to a vast empty room. And since they revolve around external witnesses, you can hear some surprising perspectives that go beyond the familiar party talking points.

Adding committees about doubled the amount of data we have, so I figured the search engine needed a bit of a facelift to deal with it. I ended up doing full reconstructive surgery. The new search does quite a bit more than its predecessor. It's not easy designing a search interface to be powerful and information-dense without also being complicated and overwhelming, and so feedback and suggestions are very welcome…

items.excerpt:
There's a MacOS app called TerminalWidget that can put terminal output in desktop widgets (I'll bet you saw that coming). Mailwidget is a shell script for creating a TerminalWidget that shows the unread count in any Mail.app mailboxes you choose.

There's a fair amount of fiddly configuration involved in making this work right, which is documented in the linked post. I did this to scratch an itch: there used to be utilities that would apply additional unread-count badges to Mail.app's icon, but those are long gone, and I wanted some approximation of that back.

You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.
